Reflexive Control.short_definition: Shaping the information another party receives so that their own reasoning leads them to a decision that benefits the sender, without their noticing.
Reflexive Control.core_meaning: Shaping the information another party receives so that their own reasoning leads them to a decision that benefits the sender, without their noticing.
Reflexive Control.expanded_definition: Reflexive control is a concept associated with Soviet and Russian military and influence theory. The idea is that a choice can be steered by shaping the picture a rival reasons from, so the rival feels it decided freely. From the receiving end, the decision looks like your own. One slanted briefing or selective news item proves little, since everyone argues from chosen facts. What marks the pattern is sustained shaping of the whole picture, plus a decision that lands conveniently for someone else. Observers can rarely prove it as it happens.
Reflexive Control.plain_language_summary: Someone arranges what you get to see so that your own careful thinking walks you to the choice they wanted. You feel you decided freely, which is why it is hard to spot.
Reflexive Control.why_this_matters: A choice we reach by our own reasoning feels like ours, so we defend it and rarely revisit it. If the inputs were selected for us, we can end up protecting a decision we never truly weighed, and finding that out later is costly.
what_it_is: A way of influencing a decision by working on what goes into the decision, not by pressuring the person who makes it.
A concept associated with Soviet and Russian military and influence theory, often described as aimed at rivals such as commanders, governments or institutions.
Open pressure and visible threats are the opposite of it, because it depends on the target believing the conclusion is self-made.
Can touch ordinary audiences when a whole information environment is tilted, though it is hard to show that any single audience was the target.
Rarely provable in the moment. Claims about it usually rest on documents or testimony that surface later.
what_it_sounds_like: A sudden run of reports, from several outlets, all pointing toward one 'obvious' course of action.
A leaked document or 'insider' tip that arrives just as a decision is due and happens to settle it.
Two options presented as the only ones, with every other path described as already ruled out.
A deadline framed as the result of events and not of anyone's choice, so the decision feels forced by facts.
Cautious voices on your own side drowned out by an alarming story that later turns out to have been thin.
Afterward, a feeling that 'everyone saw it coming' about a choice that looked surprising beforehand.
A decision-maker quoted as saying they simply followed the evidence in front of them.
what_it_is_not: Everyone decides on incomplete information, and negotiators, advertisers and friends all present the facts that favor their case. Ordinary selectivity in an argument is not a sustained effort to shape someone's whole picture.
A one-sided briefing that is labeled as advocacy, so you know whose case you are hearing.
A genuine news or intelligence failure, where sources were simply wrong or slow.
A rival's public bluff or signal, which is meant to be seen and weighed as a signal.
Hindsight, where a decision looks engineered only because you now know how it turned out.
Persuasion by open argument, where the case is stated and you can answer it.
this_may_be_it_when: Your information on a topic comes through a narrow set of channels that all trace back to one origin.
Alternatives drop out of view one by one until only one choice looks reasonable.
Documents, testimony or an investigation later show who shaped the inputs and how that fit the outcome.
Warnings that did not fit the story were hard to find or were set aside as unreliable with no explanation.
The decision benefits a party that also supplied much of the information behind it.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The inputs came from many independent sources that disagree with each other in ways you can see.
The sender states its interest openly and you weigh the claims knowing that.
The only evidence is that the outcome helped someone, which many honest outcomes do.
The surprise is explained by ordinary error, delay or confusion with no common source.
Your suspicion rests on disliking the decision, not on anything shown about where the inputs came from.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Experts and officials lean on the same few trusted sources, so their information overlaps without any plan.
Early reporting in a fast crisis is thin and often wrong, and gets fixed later.
Parties in a dispute each present their best case, as in any negotiation.
A decision can favor someone simply because interests happen to line up.
common_false_positives: A well-sourced newspaper campaign that shifts public opinion by open argument.
A government information drive that says plainly what it wants people to do.
A salesperson who highlights the features that favor a sale.
A news cycle in which every outlet covers the same story because it is big.
discernment_questions: Where did each key fact I am relying on first come from, and can I trace it past the first repeater?
How many truly independent sources agree with one another here?
Which options did I stop considering, and who told me they were off the table?
Would I make the same choice if the most dramatic piece of information turned out to be wrong?
Who gains if I choose this, and have they been open about wanting it?
less_concerning_if: You can name each source, and the sources openly disagree.
The decision is easy to reverse, so a mistake is cheap.
Corrections to earlier reports are published and the decision is revisited.
more_concerning_if: The decision is costly or hard to undo, such as a war, a major vote or a large payment.
Contrary evidence is waved away as unreliable without being addressed.
Later records show that the information was gathered or shaped by the party that gained.
pattern_over_time_signs: A single storyline keeps returning in new forms, from sources that seem unrelated.
Your list of reasonable options shrinks over weeks until one remains.
Claims that proved wrong are quietly dropped while the conclusion they supported stays.
After the decision, the evidence that favored it becomes hard to find again, or has changed.
Reflexive Control.repair_check: Correction here means the shaped inputs are named and the choice is reopened with a fuller picture. A quiet retraction of one detail, while the decision it justified stays untouched, corrects very little.
Reflexive Control.boundary_respect_check: Ask a source for the original document behind a claim and note what comes back. Handing over the primary material, and saying what it does not show, points away from steering. Vague reassurance or irritation at the question points toward it.
Reflexive Control.psychological_mechanism: A conclusion we reached ourselves feels earned, and few of us go back to audit the inputs once it does. Reasoning can only work with the facts in front of it, so a tilted set of facts can produce a sincere, confident and tilted choice. Time pressure and a shortage of independent sources can strengthen this.
Reflexive Control.possible_impact_on_receiver: A jolt of embarrassment is common on learning that facts once trusted were selected for you, along with anger and a reluctance to trust your own judgment afterward. Some become suspicious of all information, which carries its own cost. Others dig in to defend the earlier choice, because it felt like their own.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask where a key claim started: 'What is the original source for this, and has anyone independent confirmed it?' Ask it of sources you like as well as those you doubt.
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to decide under a deadline nobody can explain. Take extra time to find sources that do not trace back to the same origin before you commit.
response_options.disengagement: Step away from a flood of one-direction news about a pending decision, and come back after a day to compare it with older, slower reporting.
response_options.support_seeking: Talk the situation through with a friend who holds a different view and ask which sources they would trust. A librarian or fact-checking service can help trace where claims began.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: In an organization, ask for a written list of the sources behind a recommendation, and invite someone to argue the opposite case before a major decision is signed off.

Reflexive Control.boundary_script: "Before I act on this, where did it first come from? Who else, with no stake in it, has confirmed it? And which options have I stopped considering, and who told me to stop?"
Reflexive Control.safety_note: Reflexive control works on judgment and is not usually a direct threat to your body. That changes when a decision pushed on you involves money you cannot lose, your home, your legal status or a dangerous confrontation. Then slow down, ask a lawyer, financial counselor or trusted outside person for advice, and ask for the decision to wait.
misuse_warning: Blaming any decision you dislike on reflexive control dismisses the people who made it, and requires a hidden planner for what may be ordinary error.
Used about political opponents, it becomes a way of saying anyone who disagrees was tricked, which ends the conversation.
Reflexive Control.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Manufactured Consent works on what a whole population seems to agree with, while reflexive control concerns one party's specific decision and the facts that party was given. Computational Propaganda is a delivery method, bots and networks, which could supply inputs but says nothing about a decision. Normative Messaging leans on what others supposedly do; reflexive control leans on which facts you were shown.

Normative Messaging.short_definition: Telling people what 'most others' believe or do, so that they drift toward that apparent norm whatever they privately prefer.
Normative Messaging.core_meaning: Telling people what 'most others' believe or do, so that they drift toward that apparent norm whatever they privately prefer.
Normative Messaging.expanded_definition: Normative messaging is any communication about what is normal, common or expected in a group, from a poster saying most neighbors recycle to a headline saying everyone has moved on. People tend to adjust toward what they think others do. When the stated norm is accurate and the aim is disclosed, it is a mainstream public-health and civic tool. The concern begins when the claim is false, unverifiable or invented, or the sender hides a stake. One poster means little; the pattern is a steady drumbeat of 'everyone' claims you cannot check.
Normative Messaging.plain_language_summary: Being told that 'everybody' thinks or does something, so you go along. It is fine when the claim is true and the reason is stated, and a problem when you cannot check it.
Normative Messaging.why_this_matters: Behavior shifts to match what everyone else is said to be doing, even where private preference points elsewhere. Because the claim about what everyone does is rarely checked, a person can be moved by a majority that is smaller than described, or does not exist.
what_it_is: Messages about the typical person: 'most people in your area', 'nine in ten', 'nobody still believes that'.
Works through a wish to belong and a fear of standing out, not through argument about the merits.
Can describe what people do, or what they approve of; the second is harder to check.
Appears on posters, bills, utility letters, ads, news framing, and social feeds with visible counts.
Can be honest and helpful when the figure is accurate and the purpose is stated.
what_it_sounds_like: Most of your neighbors have already signed up.
Everyone knows that view is finished.
An ad claiming that a large crowd has already switched.
A claim that nobody serious still holds a view.
A letter comparing your energy use with 'similar households' nearby.
A feed counter showing a huge number of people agree, with no way to see who.
People like you are choosing this option.
An announcer saying 'the country has decided' before the vote.
what_it_is_not: Accurate social-norms messaging is a mainstream and often benign public-health tool. It is not manipulation when the norm stated is true and the purpose is disclosed. An unverifiable or false claim about what everyone else does is the part to notice.
A health notice that gives a correct figure from a named survey.
A friend telling you that most of your team brings lunch, so you know what to expect.
Describing a real custom to a newcomer, such as how people queue or tip.
Reporting that a view really is held by a majority, when it is.
Open advocacy with a stated purpose, such as 'join us, there are many of us'.
this_may_be_it_when: The figure has no named source, date or sample behind it.
The group called 'most people' is left vague or shifts between messages.
The claim is repeated far more than it is explained.
Dissent is described as rare or fringe without any evidence.
The pitch spends more words on belonging than on what the thing actually does.
this_may_not_be_it_when: A named survey with its method and date is linked, and you can read it.
The message states who sent it and what they want from you.
The numbers are modest and come with caveats.
Outlets with different interests report similar figures independently.
The point is a custom you are new to, offered so you can find your feet.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People say 'everyone' loosely when they mean a lot of people.
A group's custom may truly be strong where you have newly arrived.
Public agencies often use real data about behavior to encourage useful habits.
Friends mention their own choices without wanting you to copy them.
common_false_positives: A bestseller list that reports actual sales.
A poll result in a news story from a pollster that publishes its method.
A neighbor explaining how the street handles trash day.
A teacher noting that most of the class has handed the work in.
discernment_questions: Who says that most people think or do this, and how would they know?
Can I find the number itself, with a date and a sample?
Would I want this if no one else did?
Is the message describing what people do, or telling me what I ought to approve?
Does anything in it tell me what the sender gains?
less_concerning_if: The claim comes with a source you can open.
You can say no without social cost, and the message does not shame you.
The sender discloses the purpose, as an open health campaign would.
more_concerning_if: The 'majority' claim is aimed at a vote, a purchase or a heated dispute and cannot be checked.
People who doubt it are pictured as isolated, strange or disloyal.
The same 'everyone agrees' line shows up across channels with no source behind it.
pattern_over_time_signs: You catch yourself repeating 'everyone says' without remembering where you heard it.
You hesitate to state a view you hold because it feels like a minority one, though you never saw evidence that it is.
Counts and percentages shown to you keep rising while nobody can say who was counted.
When you talk to people in person, their views turn out to be more varied than the feeds suggested.
Normative Messaging.repair_check: A sender who is fixing this names the source of the figure, corrects it once it is shown to be inflated, and stops using it. A message that swaps the claim for a different 'everyone' statement has not corrected anything.
Normative Messaging.boundary_respect_check: Does asking for the source change how you are treated? Calm sharing of the survey is a good sign. Being called out of step, or told that asking is itself odd, suggests the claim leaned on pressure and not on evidence.
Normative Messaging.psychological_mechanism: Others' behavior serves as a quick guide to what is safe, correct and approved, especially in unfamiliar settings, and a norm claim borrows that shortcut. It can work even when we privately disagree, because standing out can feel costly. The effect tends to weaken when we can see the data or meet real members of the group.
Normative Messaging.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe quietly dropping a view because it seemed unpopular, feeling alone in a disagreement that was widely shared, or feeling embarrassed on finding that the majority was a fraction of what had been described. Some become wary of every statistic, including honest ones.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask politely where the figure comes from: 'Which survey is that, and when was it taken?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to change your mind or sign up on the strength of a claim about what others think until you have seen the number for yourself.
response_options.disengagement: Turn off visible counters, trending panels and 'people also' prompts for a while, and decide from what you value instead.
response_options.support_seeking: Ask two or three people you know, in person, what they actually think. Real answers are often more varied than a headline suggests.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a colleague says everyone has already agreed, ask who, and ask to hear it from them. Request that any poll be run with the question and result shared openly.

Normative Messaging.boundary_script: "Who counted these people, and when? Would I want this if I were the only one? Am I going along because it is true, or because I fear being the odd one out?"
Normative Messaging.safety_note: Norm claims are usually low-risk to your safety. The risk grows when a claim about what 'everyone' will do is used to rally a crowd against named people or to build pressure for harassment. If that appears, save the examples, report them to the platform, and contact a local support service or lawyer if you are targeted.
misuse_warning: Calling every statement about what most people think 'normative messaging' makes ordinary reporting of a true majority look sinister.
Treating a person who changed their view as sheep-like ignores that they may have been persuaded by good reasons.
Normative Messaging.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Astroturfing fakes the crowd itself, with voices that hide their sponsor; normative messaging only describes a crowd, real or not. Manufactured Consent shapes a society's agreement through media and institutions over time. Overton Window Manipulation shifts which ideas feel thinkable by pushing extremes, not by claims about what most people already think. Here, the work is done by a statement about the majority.

False Flag Operations.short_definition: Staging an attack or incident so that another group appears to be responsible, in order to justify a response or damage the blamed party.
False Flag Operations.core_meaning: Staging an attack or incident so that another group appears to be responsible, in order to justify a response or damage the blamed party.
False Flag Operations.expanded_definition: A false flag operation is an event arranged so that it looks like the work of someone else. Historians have documented some cases, usually through archives and investigations years later. In real time the label is claimed far more often than shown, because early facts about any incident are confused. A gap in the official story, an odd coincidence or a convenient result does not establish staging. What it would take is evidence about who arranged the event, which ordinary readers rarely hold.
False Flag Operations.plain_language_summary: An attack or incident is arranged to look like someone else did it, so blame, anger and action land on the wrong party. It is also a label people often apply far too fast.
False Flag Operations.why_this_matters: Retaliation, suspicion and public anger land on a group that did not do the thing, and the record that would correct it is the very thing that was arranged. The opposite harm exists too: calling real tragedies staged wounds the people who lived them.
what_it_is: A deception about who is responsible for an event, not only about what happened.
The phrase is usually traced to old naval ruses in which a ship flew another side's flag.
Cases accepted as real have been established by archives, documents, testimony and investigation, usually long after the event.
The idea can apply to a state, a group or a company, so scale does not define it.
The claim 'it was a false flag' is itself widely used to explain events people dislike, so it needs strong evidence.
what_it_sounds_like: Within hours of an incident, a confident claim that it was obviously staged by the other side.
A list of 'coincidences' offered as proof, with no document or witness behind them.
Blame assigned to a group before investigators have said anything.
Demands for a sweeping response that leans on the identity of the supposed culprit.
Posts claiming victims never existed, a common over-claim that is not evidence of staging.
Later findings that the party first named was not involved.
what_it_is_not: Most disputed events are confusing in their first days, and unanswered questions after an incident are normal, not proof of staging. Documented cases were established through archives and investigation years afterward, never through pattern-spotting in real time.
A real attack that was carried out by the group blamed for it.
Early reporting mistakes, which are common in the first days of any incident.
An accidental event whose cause stays unclear for a while, such as an industrial failure.
A group falsely claiming credit for something it did not do, which deceives about credit and not about a staged event.
Official secrecy or slow release of files, which can be poor transparency without hiding a staged event.
this_may_be_it_when: Archives, leaked documents or sworn testimony from people involved describe the arrangement.
Independent investigators with different interests reach the same conclusion about who arranged it.
Physical or digital evidence at the scene points to a source that contradicts the story given.
The blamed party's own records or witnesses credibly rule it out.
A party that gained from the blame is shown, with evidence, to have had the means and access.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The case rests on who benefited, since many events benefit someone.
The evidence is a photo or video clip whose origin you cannot trace.
Unanswered questions are being treated as proof.
Several independent bodies agree on a different explanation.
The claim says an event was staged but cannot say who, how, or what record would show it.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Casualty counts, names and timelines change as facts come in, which looks like cover-up when it is correction.
Eyewitnesses disagree honestly, because stress affects memory.
A convenient outcome can follow from honest events when unrelated interests happen to align.
Officials delay releases for legal or safety reasons.
common_false_positives: A group that carried out a real attack, denies it, and says someone else staged it.
A viral clip from a different year or place presented as proof.
An emergency drill or a film set mistaken for a real event.
A coincidence of dates between an incident and a political debate.
discernment_questions: What kind of evidence, not rumor, would show who arranged this, and has anyone with access to it said what it shows?
Is my conclusion based on a document or testimony, or only on who seems to benefit?
Would I find this convincing if the supposed culprit were a side I support instead of one I dislike?
What evidence, if it appeared, would change my mind about this?
Am I judging in the first days, before investigations have reported?
less_concerning_if: The event is recent and you hold your view loosely, waiting for investigators.
Your doubt is about one detail, not a claim that the whole event was arranged.
Multiple independent sources describe it consistently.
more_concerning_if: A claim of staging is used to justify harassing survivors or relatives.
The same claim is made across many unrelated events in the same shape.
The claim is pushed with certainty before any evidence exists.
pattern_over_time_signs: Each new incident brings the same 'it was staged' claim within hours, whatever the facts.
A theory is adjusted whenever a detail is disproved, and never dropped.
Blame follows group identity more than evidence, a pattern you may notice in your own reactions too.
Survivors or neighbors report being contacted or accused by strangers who are sure it was staged.
False Flag Operations.repair_check: When a blamed party is later shown to be innocent, correction looks like a public record that names the error, a retraction from those who spread the blame, and a plain acknowledgment to the group wrongly accused. Silence or a changed subject is not correction.
False Flag Operations.boundary_respect_check: Notice whether doubting the claim is allowed. A person confident in their evidence will show you the document and accept your questions. Anger at the question, or an accusation that you are part of the plot, suggests the claim is held on faith.
False Flag Operations.psychological_mechanism: After a shocking event, people seek a cause and a culprit, and an explanation that feels satisfying can be accepted before it is checked. Anger can narrow attention toward a group already disliked. Where trust in institutions is low, a claim that officials lied can seem plausible whether or not any evidence supports it.
False Flag Operations.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe fury at a group that may be innocent, fear of retaliation, and later shame at having shared an unverified claim. Survivors of real events describe hurt when told their loss was staged. Some people grow so wary that they cannot believe any report of an attack.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask what evidence is cited: 'Is that from a document or testimony, or is it an inference from who benefits?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to repeat a claim of staging, or of blame, until investigators or independent reporting support it, and say that you are waiting.
response_options.disengagement: Step away from fast-moving threads in the first days after an incident, when claims are least reliable, and return when fuller reporting exists.
response_options.support_seeking: Talk with someone who reads the incident differently and ask what evidence they would accept. If you are a survivor accused of faking, reach out to friends, a local support group or a lawyer.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If you edit or report news, label unverified claims of staging as unverified, and cite what investigators have actually said, with dates.

False Flag Operations.boundary_script: "I do not know who did this yet. What document, record or witness shows it, not just who benefits? Would I accept the same quality of proof if the blamed group were one I support?"
False Flag Operations.safety_note: Reading about this carries no danger. What changes that is the aftermath: a wrongly blamed group can face harassment or violence, and survivors falsely called actors can be stalked. If you or someone you know is targeted, save the messages, report them, and contact local authorities or legal aid. If danger is immediate, call emergency services.
misuse_warning: Shouting 'false flag' at any event you dislike turns a rare, evidence-based finding into a reflex, and can harm survivors and the groups blamed.
Dismissing every question about an official account as conspiracy thinking is also a misuse, since documented cases exist and asking for evidence is fair.
False Flag Operations.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Astroturfing fakes ordinary supporters; a false flag fakes an event and its author. Reflexive Control steers a rival's decision through selected information and need not stage anything. Wedge Issue Exploitation uses real divisions to fracture a coalition, with no deceit about who did what. A false flag is the one where the deception is about who stands behind a staged act.

Post-Truth Epistemic Manipulation.short_definition: Wearing down belief that facts can be established at all, until people stop trusting any source and claims cannot be held to account.
Post-Truth Epistemic Manipulation.core_meaning: Wearing down belief that facts can be established at all, until people stop trusting any source and claims cannot be held to account.
Post-Truth Epistemic Manipulation.expanded_definition: 'Post-truth' is a term for public life in which appeals to emotion and identity count for more than checkable facts. As a manipulation pattern, it means a sustained flood of contradictions, denials and 'who can really know' messages that leaves people unsure whether anything can be verified. Doubting a specific claim is healthy. This pattern pushes doubt about whether claims can be tested at all. One dishonest statement, or one sincere moment of cynicism, does not show it. What marks it is the scale and the effect: fatigue and giving up.
Post-Truth Epistemic Manipulation.plain_language_summary: People are pushed to feel that no one can know what is true, so they stop checking and stop objecting. Honest doubt about one claim is different; this is giving up on checking.
Post-Truth Epistemic Manipulation.why_this_matters: When nothing can be known, nothing can be checked, and someone left doubting everything has no ground from which to object to anything. They may also fall back on whoever sounds most certain, or on their own group.
what_it_is: A climate of doubt about whether facts can be established, not a single false claim.
Works through volume and contradiction: many stories, denials and counter-stories, so that sorting them takes more effort than most people have.
Can come from governments, parties, companies or influencers, or from ordinary audiences repeating the mood themselves, so its source is rarely clear.
Often voiced as 'both sides are the same' or 'no one can really know'.
Different from honest skepticism, which still holds that claims can be tested and wants better tests.
what_it_sounds_like: Nobody can really know what happened, so why bother?
The media lies, the experts lie, the other side lies; it is all just spin.
That's your truth; here's mine.
A dozen conflicting explanations of one event pushed at once, none withdrawn when disproved.
Accused of a lie, a speaker answers that everybody lies.
Checking a claim is mocked as naive.
A real document dismissed as 'fake' with no reason given beyond who published it.
what_it_is_not: Distrust of institutions is often earned, and saying that reporting has bias or uncertainty is honesty. The difference lies between doubting a particular claim and abandoning the idea that claims can be tested at all.
A scientist saying results are uncertain and giving the margin of error.
Reporters who correct their own mistakes in public.
Philosophical debate about knowledge, which is a serious subject and not a campaign.
Fatigue after a hard news cycle, when anyone may say 'I can't keep up'.
Healthy disagreement over what the evidence shows, with both sides citing evidence.
this_may_be_it_when: Disproved claims are replaced by new ones instead of being withdrawn, and the supply never stops.
Checking is treated as pointless or naive, regardless of what the check shows.
The message targets the idea of verification itself, not only one fact.
Contradictory stories about a single event flood in at once, and the confusion itself becomes the main result.
Real records and fake ones are treated by the speaker as equally untrustworthy.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The doubt is aimed at a specific claim and the speaker explains what evidence would settle it.
The skeptic accepts a result when the evidence is shown.
Sources disagree because the event is complex and new.
You feel worn out after heavy news, and the doubt fades with rest.
The criticism of a source gives concrete, checkable examples of past errors.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Past institutional failures give people real reasons to question official statements.
Fast news creates contradictory early reports, which is normal.
Many people say 'no one knows' as a way of staying humble about complex topics.
Algorithm-driven feeds serve conflicting content with no plan by anyone.
common_false_positives: A teacher who tells students to question every source and then shows how to check.
A friend venting 'I trust nothing now' after a scandal.
Researchers who disagree in print on a hard question.
A satirical show that mocks all sides.
discernment_questions: Am I doubting this particular claim, or have I begun to doubt that anything can be checked?
What would count as good evidence on this, and have I looked for it?
Is there anyone I trust to be right about something? Who, and why?
Who benefits when I stop checking?
Has the volume of conflicting stories left me too tired to sort them?
less_concerning_if: You can still name a few sources that have earned your trust, and say why.
Doubt leads you to look further rather than to stop.
The speaker shares how to test a claim.
more_concerning_if: You catch yourself saying nothing can be known and have stopped reading, voting or checking.
People around you treat the same record as proof or forgery depending on whose side it favors.
Pressure to give up on facts comes with encouragement to rely on one personality or group for the answers.
pattern_over_time_signs: Conflicting claims keep arriving, and few are settled before the next wave.
A growing share of conversations ends in 'you can't trust anything'.
People you know shift from 'I disagree' to 'it doesn't matter what's true'.
You notice yourself or others sharing without checking, because checking stopped seeming worth it.
Post-Truth Epistemic Manipulation.repair_check: Where trust is restored, sources publish their evidence, admit errors and let others check. A promise to be more honest next time, with no method others could test, restores very little.
Post-Truth Epistemic Manipulation.boundary_respect_check: Ask what evidence would change their mind, and listen to the answer. A concrete answer shows that claims can still be tested. 'Nothing would, they all lie' shows that the idea that testing is impossible is holding steady.
Post-Truth Epistemic Manipulation.psychological_mechanism: Faced with more contradictory claims than they can sort, many of us conserve effort by disengaging, or by retreating to the group we feel loyal to. Repeated falsehoods that carry no cost can teach that truth does not matter. Doubt can then spread from the false claim to the whole idea of checking.
Post-Truth Epistemic Manipulation.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe exhaustion, cynicism, a sense that the effort to find out is wasted, and withdrawal from news or civic life. Others describe leaning harder on one trusted voice or group because everything else feels unreliable. Some feel shame at having been fooled and stop trusting even honest sources.

response_options.soft_clarification: Separate the two doubts out loud: 'I doubt that claim, and here is what would settle it. I do not doubt that things can be checked.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to accept 'everyone lies' as an answer. Ask for the specific claim and the specific evidence, and stay on that.
response_options.disengagement: Limit how much conflicting commentary you take in. Follow a few sources with a record of corrections, and check them less often but more carefully.
response_options.support_seeking: Talk to a librarian, a teacher or a friend who enjoys checking things, and practice tracing one claim from start to finish together.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: In a team, agree on how disputed facts will be settled: which records count, who can check them, and where corrections are posted.

Post-Truth Epistemic Manipulation.boundary_script: "I can doubt this one claim without doubting everything. What would settle it, who has checked it, and have I read the original? If I cannot tell, I will say I do not know instead of pretending I do."
Post-Truth Epistemic Manipulation.safety_note: Post-truth pressure is usually not a physical danger. It matters for safety when doubt about everything leads people to ignore real warnings, such as medical, weather or financial ones. If a decision touches your health, money or home, check with a doctor, an official emergency channel or a trusted professional, not only your feed.
misuse_warning: Calling a person's honest doubt 'post-truth' can be used to shut down legitimate criticism of institutions.
Using the label for views you simply disagree with turns a description of a method into a way of saying your opponents do not care about facts.
Post-Truth Epistemic Manipulation.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Manufactured Consent tries to install an agreement; this pattern tries to dissolve the ground on which agreement or disagreement is judged. Computational Propaganda names the automated machinery that can flood a feed, while this entry names the climate of doubt that results. Overton Window Manipulation moves what is acceptable to say, not what can be known. The difference is the target: the possibility of knowing at all.
